checks.claim: Key: a thermometer reading measures the particles' average energy of motion (average kinetic energy)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a measure of the average kinetic energy of the microscopic particles'. Strictly exact for ideal gases, but for a liquid such as water at 60 C equipartition holds well for translational kinetic energy (Illinois Physics Van: 'the kinetic energies of the molecules are the same in the liquid and the gas at the same temperature'), so the school statement is true here: https://van.physics.illinois.edu/ask/listing/28547

checks.claim: Wrong: total energy of motion (that is thermal energy, which depends on amount)
Wrong: how many particles the beaker holds; how large each particle is
checks.note: Temperature is an average, independent of amount; particle size is not what a thermometer measures.

checks.claim: Context: particles at a range of speeds, some faster and some slower; total = thermal energy, depends on amount; a beaker and a drop at 60 C share one temperature
checks.note: Penn State: temperature 'measures the average kinetic energy of individual particles', thermal energy 'accounts for the total combined motion of every molecule'.

checks.claim: Key: the bathtub of warm water holds more thermal energy than a mug of boiling water, because it holds far more water
checks.note: LibreTexts: the bathtub 'contains a billion times as many water molecules' and has more total kinetic energy, yet is colder. Penn State gives the same cup-and-bathtub comparison.

checks.claim: Wrong: the mug, since hotter (confuses temperature and thermal energy)
Wrong: the bathtub, since its particles move faster (they move slower on average, being cooler)
Wrong: both the same
Context: thermal energy = total; temperature = average; mug's particles faster on average
Stem: melting ice stays at 0 C until all of it has melted, then the temperature climbs
checks.note: OpenStax: 'The temperature of a cup of soda initially at 0C stays at 0C until all the ice has melted.'

checks.claim: Key: the energy goes into freeing particles from the solid, not speeding them up
checks.note: Grokipedia: energy is needed to 'break or form the intermolecular bonds that hold the substance in its current phase' 'without altering the average kinetic energy of the molecules'. OpenStax: 'the cohesive bonds between the molecules in the solid must be broken apart'. 'Freeing particles' from their fixed places is a fair grade-7 wording (liquid particles stay close but move past each other), and the context says exactly that.

checks.claim: Wrong: speeding particles up (would raise the temperature)
Wrong: into the beaker's glass, not the ice
checks.note: The glass in contact with stirred ice water also stays near 0 C; the heat passes through it into melting the ice.

checks.claim: Wrong: swelling the particles (particles do not grow; ice in fact shrinks as it melts)
Stem: a metal (brass) ball passes through its ring when both are cool; heated alone it no longer goes through
checks.note: Toronto: heat the ball until it 'no longer goes through the ring'. Stony Brook and Harvard's demo use a brass ball and ring: https://www.stonybrook.edu/commcms/physics-lab-demo/i.-thermodynamics/i1.-thermal-properties-of-matter/thermal_expansion_ball_and_ring.php ; https://sciencedemonstrations.fas.harvard.edu/presentations/thermal-expansion

checks.claim: Key: its particles move (vibrate) faster and sit farther apart on average
checks.note: Grokipedia: expansion comes from 'enhanced vibrational motion of atoms or molecules as their kinetic energy rises with temperature', so the average spacing grows.

checks.claim: Wrong: each particle has swollen larger (a listed misconception)
Wrong: a fluid of heat (caloric) has soaked in; Context: caloric held by many scientists of the late 1700s, pushed particles apart, given up in the 1800s once heat was shown to be energy
checks.note: Grokipedia: Lavoisier and Laplace formalized caloric in the 1780s; caloric 'entered the spaces between particles and pushed them apart'; Rumford 1798, Joule 1840s, and by the 1850s Clausius and Thomson made it obsolete.

checks.claim: Wrong: particles from the flame have joined its own
checks.note: Expansion is a change in spacing, not added matter.

checks.claim: Stem: bridge expansion joints spanned by interlocking steel teeth (finger joints)
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'Finger joints, composed of interlocking steel plates, are designed for larger displacements'.

checks.claim: Key: in summer the gap is narrower because the bridge has expanded (grown longer)
checks.note: Arizona DOT: the joint opens in winter when the concrete contracts; an Atlantis Press bridge study found summer heat lengthens the girder and shrinks the joint to its minimum width; SlashGear: gaps feel larger in winter when the concrete shrinks.

checks.claim: Wrong: wider because shorter; wider because the gap itself grows; the same because concrete cannot grow
checks.note: Concrete expands with heat; joints let bridges change length without buckling.

checks.claim: Context: joints let a bridge change length without buckling; jointed rails have small gaps for the same reason
checks.note: Grokipedia: jointed rail uses gaps of about 1/4 to 1/2 inch at rail ends to allow expansion and contraction and prevent buckling.

checks.claim: Key: the metal lid expands more than the glass
checks.note: HyperPhysics: 'the thermal expansion coefficient of the metal is greater than that of the glass' (steel about 1.44 times glass); 'Directing the stream of hot water at the center of the lid heats the metal more than the glass'. Grokipedia's table: steel 12, aluminium 23, soda-lime glass 9 (x10^-6 per K); lab borosilicate glass expands even less.

checks.claim: Wrong: the glass expands more than the lid; the glass rim shrinks when heated
checks.note: Glass expands less than steel or aluminium, and it expands (not shrinks) when heated.

checks.claim: Wrong: hot water makes the metal lid softer
checks.note: Metal lids (steel, aluminium at about 660 C melting) are unaffected in hardness by water below 100 C. (Hot water can soften the rubbery liner seal, but the choice names the metal itself, so it stays wrong.)

checks.claim: Context: water heats the lid faster than the glass beneath; glass expands too, only less
Stem: Galileo made an early thermoscope in Padua
checks.note: Museo Galileo: 'invented by Galileo during his stay in Padua'; Viviani gives 1597, Grokipedia around 1592-1603 (date uncertain). The stem gives no date, so it is safe. Grokipedia credits Galileo with the earliest known construction: https://grokipedia.com/page/Thermoscope

checks.claim: Stem: a bulb the size of a hen's egg with a long thin neck, turned upside down with the open end in water
checks.note: Castelli (letter of 20 Sept 1638): 'a glass flask the size of a small hen's egg with a neck around two palms in length and as thin as a barley-stalk', mouth inverted into a vessel of water.

checks.claim: Key: when warmer, the water sank, pushed down by the expanding air
checks.note: Grokipedia: warming expands the air and pushes water down the tube; cooling draws it up (Castelli saw it rise as the flask cooled).

checks.claim: Wrong: rose, drawn up by warming air; rose as warmed water expanded; stayed put
checks.note: Gases expand far more than liquids (ideal gas about 0.0037 per K vs water's roughly 0.0002), so the air's expansion dominates and the level falls; glass conducts heat and does not keep it out.

checks.claim: Context: opposite way to a modern thermometer; in a liquid-in-glass thermometer the liquid expands more than the glass and climbs
checks.note: Grokipedia: the liquid expands more than the glass bulb and rises up a narrow calibrated tube.

checks.claim: Stem: wet- and dry-bulb thermometers side by side in a weather shelter, wet one wrapped in water-soaked cloth in moving air, reading several degrees lower
checks.note: Grokipedia: a bulb 'covered with a wet wick exposed to airflow' reads cooler; equal only at 100% relative humidity. Stevenson screens commonly house 'dry- and wet-bulb hygrometers' with air passing through the louvres: https://grokipedia.com/page/Stevenson_screen

checks.claim: Key: the fastest water particles escape, carrying energy off
checks.note: Grokipedia: molecules have 'a distribution of kinetic energies'; the most energetic escape and 'the average kinetic energy of the remaining liquid decreases'.

checks.claim: Wrong: water gives off cold (cold is not a substance); water shields the bulb; wet glass reads falsely low
checks.note: Heat/cold as substances is a listed grades 5-8 misconception. The wet-bulb reading is a real temperature, used with the dry bulb in a psychrometer to calculate relative humidity (Grokipedia, Wet-bulb temperature).

checks.claim: Context: slower particles left behind, the water colder, draws heat from the bulb; observers compare the two to measure humidity
Stem: William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed in 1848 the scale scientists still use, measured in kelvins, with a degree the same size as a degree Celsius
checks.note: Thomson's 1848 paper ('On an Absolute Thermometric Scale', Phil. Mag., Oct 1848) proposed a FIRST absolute scale built on Carnot's caloric theory; its 0 and 100 were set at water's freezing and boiling points ('The arbitrary points which coincide on the two scales are 0 and 100'), and its degrees matched the air thermometer's only there. Wikipedia (Kelvin): that 1848 scale was logarithmic with absolute zero at minus infinity, and the scale used today was formulated by Thomson and Joule in 1854: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin . Grokipedia and many school sources repeat '1848', but the primary source contradicts the stem as written. Fix: 'William Thomson, a physicist later made Lord Kelvin, worked out in the mid-1800s a temperature scale that scientists still use, measured in kelvins.' (or say 'in 1854').

checks.claim: A kelvin is the same size as a degree Celsius; the Kelvin scale has no negative temperatures; 0 C = 273.15 K
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'a temperature interval of 1 K equals 1 C'; the scale 'prohibits negative temperatures'. (Since 1967-68 the unit is the kelvin, not 'degree Kelvin'; 'a degree on his scale' is a loose but harmless child-level phrase.)

checks.claim: Key: 0 K stands for the coldest temperature anything can have (absolute zero, about -273 C)
checks.note: 'the lowest possible temperature', 0 K = -273.15 C.

checks.claim: Wrong: water freezes at about 273 K, not 0
Wrong: empty outer space is about 2.7 K, not 0 (CMB, radiation left from the early universe)
checks.note: CMB 2.7255 K, 'the thermal remnant radiation from the Big Bang'.

checks.claim: Wrong / Context: coldest air recorded on Earth about -89 C
checks.note: -89.2 C at Vostok Station, 21 July 1983 (satellite surface low -93.2 C, 2010). Both far above absolute zero.

checks.claim: Stem: physicists have chilled atoms to less than a billionth of a degree above absolute zero
checks.note: 2021: a rubidium condensate in free fall at the Bremen drop tower reached an effective 38 picokelvin (0.038 billionths). Even setting that 'effective' figure aside, MIT (Ketterle, 2003) cooled sodium atoms to about 450-500 pK, 'half-a-billionth of a degree': https://news.mit.edu/2003/cooling . The wording survives any new record, since records only go lower. (Grokipedia's Absolute zero page misattributes the 38 pK record to rhodium demagnetization; the wording here is unaffected.)

checks.claim: Key: at absolute zero particles have the least energy possible
checks.note: Grokipedia: at absolute zero a system's 'internal energy reaches its minimum'; zero-point energy means motion never wholly stops (Grokipedia, Absolute zero).

checks.claim: Wrong: particles there are all locked in solids (helium stays liquid at ordinary pressure)
checks.note: Grokipedia: helium-4 'does not solidify upon cooling to absolute zero at low pressures'; needs about 25 atm. Wikipedia agrees ('does not solidify at normal pressure').

checks.claim: Wrong: no thermometer can read lower; scientists agreed to end the scale there
checks.note: The limit is physical (minimum energy; third law), not instrumental or conventional.

checks.claim: Context: a tiny quantum jiggle remains (zero-point energy)
Context: Guillaume Amontons estimated it in 1703 from the way air presses less as it cools
checks.note: Wikipedia and Grokipedia both give 1703: the zero of his air thermometer was the temperature 'at which the spring of the air was reduced to nothing', equivalent to about -240 C. (Wikipedia adds he held it unreachable and never computed it explicitly; 'estimated' is still a fair summary, since his scale's zero placed it.)

unit_notes: 9 ok, 1 error. The error is historical: the scale in kelvins starting at absolute zero is Thomson's later (1854, with Joule) scale, not his 1848 one, whose 0 and 100 sat at water's freezing and boiling points. The physics in every question checks out; temperature as average kinetic energy is safe here (liquid water, where translational equipartition holds well).
